title: Dynamic Evaluation of Neural Mechanisms for Affective Touch: Pathways for Touch-induced Pleasantness and Pain Modulation
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because the research findings will elucidate mechanisms for
effects of slow stroking and deep pressure – components of massage therapy – on touch pleasantness and
pain modulation. The proposed research will also characterize a novel pathway for affective deep pressure and
elucidate its peripheral and central mechanisms, opening new horizons in mechanistic research on massage.
The project is relevant to NCCIH’s mission because it addresses fundamental, real-time mechanistic
processes of components of massage therapy.

title: NCANDA: Data Analysis Resource - Upgrading Software
text:
This supplement requests funds to upgrade the software of the Scalable Informatics for Biomedical Imaging
Studies (SIBIS), which is used by the National Consortium on Alcohol and Neurodevelopment in Adolescence
(NCANDA) study for data acquisition, management, quality control, harmonization, analysis, and distribution to
the public. The goal of NCANDA is to follow youth who have and have not engaged in hazardous drinking to
determine alcohol's influence on the brain, cognition, emotion, and life activities in emerging adulthood when
young men and women are establishing themselves in careers, relationships, and independent living.
Upgrading the SIBIS software will enable us to maintain its high level of digital security so that NCANDA can
continue with securely tracking its participants, whose longitudinal data are critical to better understand how
heavy alcohol drinking during adolescence impacts this period of life and adult functioning.

title: Actin methylation as a novel mechanism that regulates gut barrier integrity and repair
text:
RELEVANCE TO PUBLIC HEALTH
Intestinal disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease and infectious colitis represent a
serious health problem in the US with their incidence and complications accelerating over the past decades.
This project will improve upon the understanding of normal gut physiology and the pathogenesis of
gastrointestinal disorders by exploring novel mechanisms that regulate integrity of the gut barrier, development
of intestinal inflammation and post-inflammatory mucosal restitution. Furthermore, it will identify a novel target
for pharmacological prevention of the intestinal barrier breakdown and accelerated healing of the injured gut
mucosa, which would result in decreased morbidity and mortality of a large cohort of patients with inflammatory
disorders.

title: Core 4 - Genome Sequencing Core
text:
The core will perform high output whole genome bulk and single cell sequencing, uniformly analyze clinical 
sample both to investigate for genomic changes in MM at the time of diagnosis and at relapse and correlate 
changes in MM with various clinical groups as well as identify clonal complexity and variations and mutational 
signatures operative in myeloma.

title: Modeling Best Approaches for Cardiovascular Disease Prevention in Cancer Survivors
text: The goal of this proposal is to identify optimal strategies for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD) for survivors of breast (BC), prostate (PC) and lung (LC) cancer by developing and validating a novel Integrated Multi-Ethnic Cancer model (IMEC) to incorporate the development, progression, and outcomes of CVD among a representative population of BC, PC and LC survivors. We will then assess the effectiveness and cost- effectiveness (CE) of different primary CVD prevention strategies for this large group of cancer survivors (>6 million in the US). The study will be innovative in applying state-of-the-art modeling approaches to evaluate primary CVD prevention strategies in a varied population of cancer survivors, an understudied group at risk for poorer outcomes, and our results will have direct implications for the management of large numbers of cancer survivors and guide patient decision-making.

title: Cancer Molecular Imaging, Nanotechnology, and Theranostics (CMINT)
text: CANCER MOLECULAR IMAGING, NANOTECHNOLOGY, AND THERANOSTICS (CMINT) RESEARCH PROGRAM ABSTRACT The primary objective of the UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center (JCCC) Cancer Molecular Imaging, Nanotechnology, and Theranostics (CMINT) Research Program is to advance translational imaging, nanoparticle design and delivery, and theranostics with the goal of improving cancer patient outcomes. The Program is led by Director Johannes Czernin, MD, and Co-Directors Caius Radu, MD, and Jeffrey Zink, PhD. CMINT has 50 members from 19 departments located within five UCLA schools and affiliate institution Caltech. Program members possess a wide range of synergistic expertise in biology, immunology, nuclear medicine, physics, nanotechnology, urology, radiology, radiation oncology, drug development, engineering, image reconstruction, chemistry, radiochemistry, and animal models of disease. As of 3/1/2024 the Program was supported by $12.4M in direct cost funding, of which $6.4M (51%) is from the NCI and $11.3M (91%) is peer-reviewed. CMINT discoveries led to 952 publications from 2019 – 2023, of which 25% and 35% are intra- and inter-programmatic collaborations, respectively, while 34% result from collaborations with other NCI-designated cancer centers. High impact (IF ≥10) journal publications are 38%. An example of impactful CMINT Program science since 2019 is leadership in two FDA-approved New Drug Applications (NDAs) for a theranostics pair targeting Prostate Specific Membrane Antigen (PSMA), transforming prostate cancer management, diagnostics, and patient care, a priority cancer in the Los Angeles County (LAC) catchment area. Four Specific Aims advance the Program’s objectives: (1) To develop advanced instrumentation, analytical tools, and molecular imaging approaches to investigate tumor biology in vivo; (2) To explore novel nanotechnology-based systems to enable precise immunomodulatory agent delivery and diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring; (3) To investigate immune responses and immunotherapy using novel molecular imaging approaches; and (4) To pursue clinical theranostic approaches, evaluate new theranostic targets, conduct large-scale imaging trials, and overcome resistance mechanisms through rational combination therapies. Program members continue leading the advance of Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging towards precision theranostics while building strength in translatable imaging technologies and methodologies. CMINT is committed to training the next generation of cancer researchers, with additional activities with this focus since 2019, including developing and launching in summer 2024 an Imaging and Theranostics Summer Fellowship Program that recruits students from area high schools. CMINT research goals are described in and align with Key Aim 3 of the current 2019 – 2023 and refreshed 2024 – 2028 JCCC Strategic Plans. Program activities collaborate and synergize with JCCC Community Outreach and Engagement (COE) and Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination (CRTEC) units, and utilize essential JCCC Shared Resources to achieve Program objectives while also meeting the priorities and evolving needs of LAC residents and communities.

title: Clinical Decision Support for Early Detection of Deterioration in Hospitalized Children
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on developing a novel, accurate,
interpretable, and user-friendly clinical decision support tool for predicting cardiopulmonary deterioration in
hospitalized children. Once accomplished, this research work will result in an actionable tool for early detection
and of deteriorating children, thereby facilitating timely intervention and improvement of outcomes. Thus, the
proposed research is relevant to the part of NIH’s mission that pertains to enhancing health, lengthening life, and
reducing illness and disability.

title: Individualizing Steroid Use in Pneumonia
text:
Pneumonia remains the leading infectious cause of death. Presently doctors do not know which patients can
benefit from steroids, when to give steroids, or how much steroid to give. In this application, we propose an
approach to steroid use in pneumonia that considers an individual’s unique features, seeking to give the right
dose of steroid to the right patient and at the right time.

title: Decoding time-dependent nonlinearities underlying responses to natural stimuli
text:
Decades of vision neuroscience research using artificial stimuli designed to isolate specific
visual processing features has failed to translate into understanding responses to natural
stimuli—the inputs for which the visual system evolved. The proposed work will identify time-
dependent nonlinearities across multiple circuit levels and timescales and how these
nonlinearities interact. These findings will be used to develop biologically-inspired models that
accurately predict retinal responses to naturalistic inputs. This research is essential for
understanding normal vision, designing effective retinal prostheses, and identifying the
mechanisms underlying visual deficits in retinal disease.

title: Towards a Genetic Atlas of the Plain People in Western Pennsylvania: Improving Diagnosis, Access, and Health Outcomes
text:
This study seeks to address the pressing healthcare disparities faced by the rapidly growing Plain people (Amish
and Mennonites) in western Pennsylvania, who are at higher risk for certain genetic disorders. We aim to identify
new genetic conditions and assess the prevalence of genetic conditions within this community to facilitate
targeted screening, improve health outcomes through early detection, and increase healthcare access while
reducing costs. This research will not only pave the way for improved healthcare outcomes for the Plain people
but will also provide broader lessons that can benefit both the Plain and the general population.

title: Biostatistics & Informatics Shared Resource
text: BIOSTATISTICS AND INFORMATICS SHARED RESOURCE (BISR): ABSTRACT The Biostatistics and Informatics Shared Resource (BISR) plays an essential role in the research activities of The University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) by supporting the data science needs of KUCC investigators. The BISR is co-led by Byron Gajewski (CPC), PhD, and Devin Koestler (CB), PhD, both accomplished biostatisticians with a long-standing commitment to cross-disciplinary collaborations. The BISR includes 19 faculty members with specialized cancer biostatistics research expertise, 13 technical support staff and postdoctoral fellows, and three administrative staff members who provide additional technical and administrative expertise, adding efficiency to the resource. The BISR assists KUCC investigators by providing guidance and direction in study design, statistical oversight and analyses, clinical research informatics and data management, electronic data collection, bioinformatics, complex data set (statistical ‘omics) analysis, and investigator-initiated clinical trials. The BISR consists of faculty and staff whose diverse expertise and skill sets span the areas of biostatistics, bioinformatics, and informatics. The considerable overlap between these three areas allows researchers to work with a single shared resource for their data collection, analytics, and statistical analysis needs. The synergy between the areas that encompass “data science” enables the BISR to support a wide range of quality services in a timely and cost-effective manner. To support the research activities of KUCC members, the specific aims of this resource are to: 1) provide study design and statistical support and expertise; 2) provide bioinformatics and statistical genetics support and expertise; 3) provide informatics expertise for data collection and management, as well as develop and support ongoing research enabling technologies, platforms, and tools; and 4) educate students, fellows and faculty members of KUCC on data science, reproducible research ideas, and methods used in cancer research. From 2016-2020, the BISR supported 69, 60, 85, 80, and 78 KUCC members respectively. In 2020, the breakdown was 18, 33, and 27 members from Cancer Biology, Cancer Prevention and Control, and Drug Discovery, Delivery and Experimental Therapeutics, respectively, on 89 grant applications (submissions and resubmissions) and 161 projects (ongoing grants, IITs, and other projects). In addition, the BISR supported 31 non-member cancer researchers in 2020. For all cancer-related projects, the BISR supported 340 grant applications plus projects in 2020. In 2021, CCSG funding accounts for ~10% of the BISR budget, with an annual direct support return on investment of approximately $0.6M dollars in external funding to support BISR faculty and staff (31% of BISR support).

title: Creating cancer-specific genotoxicity by targeting Cas9 nickase to focal gene amplifications
text:
Focal gene amplification is a hallmark of many types of cancer that drives tumorigenesis, such as
MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma. Gene amplification affords an opportunity for therapeutic
exploitation if DNA damage can be site-specifically targeted to amplified loci, since the damage
will accumulate specifically in cancer cells. DNA nicks (single strand breaks, SSBs) can create
single ended double strand breaks (seDSBs) within a proliferating cell if encountered by a DNA
replication fork, where large numbers of seDSBs can lead to cell death. SpCas9 nickase can be
employed to selectively create large numbers of SSBs within the genome of proliferating cancer
cells by targeting highly amplified loci resulting in a toxic level of seDSBs. MYCN-amplified
neuroblastoma provides an ideal cancer to test the efficacy of Cas9 nickase as a cancer-selective
genotoxic agent when targeting focal gene amplification. MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma is
observed in ~20% of diagnosed cases and has an overall survival rate of ~50%. Thus, it
represents a target with important unmet medical need. Based on our preliminary data, Cas9
nickase shows promise as a selective therapeutic agent for MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells
in vitro and in vivo. We propose to improve the properties of Cas9 nickase for selective killing of
MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma cells and demonstrate its therapeutic potential in vivo in an
orthotopic xenograft model of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma. In Aim 1, we will optimize the
efficiency of neuroblastoma cell killing by Cas9 nickase through improvements to the nickase,
sgRNA and choice of target site. In Aim 2, we will optimize our lipid nanoparticle carrier formulation
for delivery of Cas9 nickase mRNA to an orthotopic xenograft model of neuroblastoma and
evaluate the efficacy of tumor reduction by Cas9 nickase. In Aim 3, we will evaluate small
molecule inhibitors of DNA damage response pathways for their ability to enhance Cas9 nickase
toxicity. We have already demonstrated that Cas9 nickase toxicity is enhanced by a CHK1
inhibitor, which blocks a DNA damage response pathway that responds to cellular replication
stress. We will then evaluate the efficacy of tumor reduction in vivo by Cas9 nickase in conjunction
with promising inhibitors of DNA damage response pathways. At the conclusion of this study, we
will have a therapeutic lead for the treatment of refractory MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma that
can undergo further optimization, and efficacy and safety assessments in vitro and in vivo in the
context of assembling a pre-IND package for FDA interactions.

title: Advanced Genetic Engineering to Unravel Tumor-Specific B Cell Responses
text:
Tumor-infiltrating B-cells (TIBs) have been described in various solid tumors and constitute the 3rd most
abundant tumor-infiltrating cells. TIBs often form immune compartments called tertiary lymphoid structures
(TLS), where T-cells are activated through B-cell signaling and their professional antigen-presenting function.
We hypothesized that gene editing could be exploited to redirect the specificity of the endogenous BCR toward
the tumor antigens to study the role of antigen-specific B cell responses in tumors and ultimately develop novel
immunotherapy strategies. The efficacy of this adoptive treatment will be evaluated in vivo in breast cancer
mouse models. This in-vivo immunization strategy will redirect both the humoral and cellular immunity against
solid tumors, introducing new avenues for empowered cancer-adoptive immunotherapies.

title: Elucidating Lipid Binding Preferences of Membrane Proteins Using Mass Spectrometry
text:
Membrane proteins are essential regulators of cellular function, yet key aspects of their activity remain poorly understood
due to limited information about their natural lipid-binding preferences. In this project, I will develop an integrated
approach that combines native mass spectrometry (MS) with advanced tandem MS techniques to confidently identify the
specific lipids that are associated with membrane proteins under native-like conditions. The identification of these lipid
species will enable further studies on how high-affinity lipids affect the structure and function of membrane proteins, thus
advancing our understanding of their regulatory mechanisms and potential as therapeutic targets.

title: Global Infectious Diseases Research Training Program
text:
The University at Buffalo (UB)/State University of New York (SUNY), Upstate Medical University (Upstate/SUNY)
and The University of the West Indies (UWI) Mona Campus (Kingston, Jamaica), in collaboration with the
Jamaica Ministry of Health, are applying to renew the current Global Infectious Diseases (GID) Research
Training Program with a continued focus on virology research training and capacity building. The research
training is focused on the priority areas for public health in Jamaica and will create a workforce with skills to seek
peer-reviewed funding and build an independent research program.

title: Developmental Biology and Solid Tumor Program (DBSTP)
text: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT – DEVELOPMENTAL BIOLOGY AND SOLID TUMOR PROGRAM Children with advanced or recurrent solid tumors have poor cure rates, and those who are cured are at an increased risk of chronic medical conditions. The goal of the Developmental Biology and Solid Tumor Program (DBSTP) is to improve the survival and quality of life of children with solid tumors by integrating basic, clinical, and survivorship research. Michael Dyer, PhD (Laboratory Research Lead) and Alberto Pappo, MD (Clinical Research Lead) are responsible for the overall leadership, academic themes, and direction of the DBSTP. They meet weekly to coordinate the Program’s activities, identify clinical translation opportunities, and plan clinical trials. They also mentor Program members, identifying and removing barriers to collaboration among St. Jude Comprehensive Cancer Center (SJCCC) members and with investigators around the world who share their goal of improving survival and quality of life for children with solid tumors. DBSTP holds a weekly seminar series to provide a forum for every Program member and invited speakers from other NCI-designated Cancer Centers to present their research. To strengthen the Program’s basic, translational, and clinical research endeavors over the past project period, new members have been recruited to align with three thematic areas: Precision Medicine, Cancer Immunotherapy, and Translational Research. In response to feedback from the prior renewal, Dyer and Pappo now engage in annual strategic planning and have developed a personalized, targeted mentoring program, resulting in a 37% increase of peer-reviewed cancer-focused funding. To further strengthen the Program’s translational research, the DBSTP supported the successful U01 application to join the NCI Pediatric Preclinical In Vivo Testing Program. Program members serve as principal investigators on 18 institutional clinical trials and 26 Children’s Oncology Group or industry-sponsored trials. Investigator-initiated trials for frontline treatment of rhabdomyosarcoma, non-rhabdomyosarcoma soft-tissue sarcomas, and neuroblastoma and protocols for relapsed neuroblastoma and Ewing sarcoma will ensure continued robust trial enrollment that will accelerate the development of new therapies. The DBSTP has 31 members (25 full and six Early Career Investigators), representing 12 departments. During the project period, research from the DBSTP has resulted in 517 publications, of which 34% are intraprogrammatic (a 48% increase in intraprogrammatic collaborations), 43% are interprogrammatic, and 76% are interinstitutional (with other NCI-designated Cancer Centers). The DBSTP contributed 807 interventional enrollments: 145 participants in national, 594 in institutional, and 68 in industry-sponsored trials. Accrual to therapeutic trials has more than doubled since FY21, reaching similar numbers as those seen pre-COVID.

title: Develop Conditionally Armored CAR Macrophage Therapy for Pancreatic Cancer
text:
Patients with advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma desperately need novel and effective therapeutics.
Macrophage allotransplantation seems permissive, making them a safe choice as a “third-party, off-the-shelf”
cell therapy option. The proposed research will not only provide a proof-of-concept regarding the combination
therapy of KRAS inhibitors and macrophages genetically engineered with chimeric antigen receptors and pro-
inflammatory cytokines, but will also enhance the understanding of macrophage self-renewal, plasticity, signaling
transduction and function execution.

title: Physicochemical control of multilineage emergence
text:
Project Narrative.
The goal of this project is to use human induced pluripotent stem cells, micropatterned culture, synthetic
biomaterial scaffolds, and microfluidics, to recreate the dynamic microenvironmental cues that coax tissue self-
assembly and maturation. We anticipate that this holistic approach will enhance our understanding of multi-
germ layer communication in lineage specification, as well as the role of mechanical and chemical cues in
directing stem cell fate. Collectively, these approaches will build a framework for elucidating the mechanisms of
human development and improve stem cell models of morphogenesis and disease.

title: Mitochondrial Imaging, PTM Analysis & Metabolism Core
text:
RELEVANCE:
High-resolution imaging of the mitochondria, analyses of cell metabolism and PTMs as well as cell, tissue, and
plasma metabolites are integral to the success of each of the PPG Projects. These services are best centralized
given their inherent difficulty, reliance on specialized and sophisticated equipment and expertise, as well as the
requirements of all three projects. Core B will provide these services for all three projects.
